area: Technics SX-WSA1R — Universal / General MIDI System Exclusive (receive and transmit), from the annotated TLCS-900 disassembly at /home/fsanches/compartilhado/kn5000-roms-disasm/wsa1

findings.topic: HEADLINE: only TWO universal SysEx messages are recognised — GM System On and GM System Off
findings.detail: Walking the firmware's own SysEx match table end to end, the complete set of Universal System Exclusive messages the WSA1R acts on is: GM System On and GM System Off, both addressed to device 0x7F (all-call). Nothing else universal is decoded — see the separate 'not recognised' finding for the enumeration that proves it. Everything else the SysEx engine understands is Matsushita-ID (0x50) traffic.

findings.topic: GM System On — exact bytes and exactly what it changes
findings.detail: On receipt the handler at 0xFB51E7 does three things, unconditionally: (1) `set 7,(0x60F020)` — a flag byte in the 0x60F000 scratch page, purpose not established; (2) `or (0x7F4D),0x04` — SETS BIT 2 of the byte at RAM 0x7F4D, which is the machine's global GENERAL MIDI MODE flag; (3) posts a four-field record {E=0x91, D=0x03, A=the new value of (0x7F4D), W=0x04} onto the pending UI/parameter event list at 0x2E00. It does not itself reload any sound settings; the 'replace your current settings with GENERAL MIDI settings' work is done by whatever consumes event 0x91/0x03.

findings.topic: GM System Off — exact bytes, and it is a no-op when GM mode is already off
findings.detail: The handler at 0xFB520C first reads (0x7F4A + 3) = (0x7F4D) and tests bit 2 with `and C,0x04`. If the bit is already clear it returns immediately — no flag write, no event posted. Otherwise it sets bit 7 of (0x60F020), clears bit 2 of (0x7F4D) with `and (XIX+3),0xFB`, and posts the same {E=0x91, D=0x03, A=new (0x7F4D), W=0x04} record. So a second GM System Off in a row is silently ignored, while a second GM System On is not (the On handler has no such guard).

findings.topic: Bit 2 of RAM 0x7F4D IS the GENERAL MIDI MODE flag (corroborated four independent ways)
findings.detail: The one thing GM On/Off change is bit 2 of the byte at 0x7F4D. That this bit is the user-visible 'GENERAL MIDI MODE : ON/OFF' setting is corroborated by: (a) the panel screen object at PanelScreen_VtableTable entry 0x9A / screen id 0x7A, whose painter's own text reads 'GENERAL MIDI', ' GENERAL MIDI MODE  :  ', ' ON', ' OFF'; (b) prom_b routines that set and clear exactly this bit and then post the identical {0x91, 0x03, value, 0x04} record; (c) three Standard-MIDI-File writers that choose which GM System message to embed by testing `bit 2,(0x7f4d)`; (d) many read-only consumers across prom_b.

findings.topic: Where the message is decoded: a byte-trie whose FIRST level matches the THIRD byte of the message
findings.detail: The SysEx body parser (sub_FB63D1) skips two bytes — the 0xF0 and the ID byte — then walks a trie of 6-byte records [match:1][action:1][next:u32]. Level 1 is the sub-array that starts at 0xF5115B; each matched byte is stored in the 16-byte parse record at (0x60FCD8) at offsets 5,6,7,...; a non-zero action byte ends the walk and becomes the command number in record slot 0. For the universal branch the three levels are: device-ID byte, then sub-ID#1, then sub-ID#2. Level 1: 0x7F, action 0, next 0x00F4FFCD. Level 2: 0x09, action 0, next 0x00F4FFBB. Level 3: 0x01 -> action 0x20 (command 32 = GM System On); 0x02 -> action 0x21 (command 33 = GM System Off). Command N is then dispatched through a 34-entry pointer table.

findings.topic: The device-ID byte must be 0x7F exactly — there is no per-unit device number and no wildcard at that level
findings.detail: Level 1 of the trie compares the byte only for equality and for the 0xFF end-of-list marker; the 0xFE 'match anything' wildcard that levels 2 and deeper support is NOT implemented at level 1. The level-1 list contains 0x7F and no other value that could serve as a device ID. So `F0 7E 00 09 01 F7`, `F0 7E 10 09 01 F7`, etc. are NOT recognised — only the 0x7F all-call form is.

findings.topic: NOT recognised: Master Volume, Identity Request/Reply, GM2 On, and every other universal message
findings.detail: Two independent gates rule these out. (1) The MIDI front end accepts only two ID bytes after 0xF0 — 0x50 and 0x7E — so every Universal REAL-TIME message (0xF0 0x7F ...), which is where GM Master Volume (F0 7F 7F 04 01 ll mm F7) and Master Balance live, is discarded before it ever reaches the body parser. (2) Inside the Universal Non-Real-Time branch the only sub-ID#1 in the table is 0x09; there is no 0x06 (Identity / General Information), no 0x01-0x05 (sample dump / file dump), no 0x08 (tuning), no 0x04, and under 0x09 only sub-ID#2 0x01 and 0x02 — so no GM2 System On (0x03). A whole-ROM byte scan finds no 7E 7F 06, no 7E 00 06 and no 7F 7F 04 anywhere in prom_a/prom_b/prom_c. The unit therefore never answers an Identity Request.

findings.topic: GM On/Off are NOT subject to the per-command receive filter
findings.detail: Before dispatch, sub_FB6B87 looks the command number up in a 34-byte class table at 0xF4FE82 and, for classes 1, 2 and 3, requires the matching bits of (0x7FD6) to be set — otherwise it writes error 0x21 into parse-record slot 4 and the message is dropped. Commands 32 and 33 (GM On/Off) have class byte 0x00, which matches none of the three tests, so the routine falls straight through and the messages are always honoured regardless of (0x7FD6). Three further pre-dispatch gates (sub_FB6BF4, sub_FB6CFC, sub_FB6DBD) test only command numbers 0x11/0x14/0x18/0x1A and first-bytes 0x7E/0x2B/0x2C/0x2D, none of which is the GM path.

findings.topic: The receive framing: which bytes must be present, and where the message is assembled
findings.detail: Two identical state machines drain two rings. Each waits for 0xF0 (state 0), then requires the next byte to be 0x50 or 0x7E (state 1, anything else aborts the message), then accumulates data bytes until a byte with bit 7 set arrives; that byte must be 0xF7 or the message is aborted. Every accumulated byte, including the leading 0xF0, the ID and the closing 0xF7, goes into the buffer through sub_FB6165. On 0xF7 the trie walk and dispatch run. So the recognised form really is the full six-byte F0 ... F7, not a fragment.

findings.topic: Both MIDI receive paths reach the same handlers
findings.detail: Ring 0x601646 is filled by the INTERRUPT-time parser (MIDI_RX_SysExStart / MIDI_RX_SysExData / the 0xF7 arm of MIDI_RX_Byte, all via Ring601646_Put 0xF41E3C); ring 0x601C6E is filled by the FOREGROUND parser (MIDI_Fg_SystemCommon / MIDI_Fg_SysExData via Ring601C6E_PutBlock 0xF41EAC and Ring601C6E_Put 0xF41EA8). The main loop drains both on every pass. Their two dispatch tables differ for the Matsushita commands (PtrTable_F4F800 sends commands 1-8 and 10-22 to 0xFB2820, PtrTable_F4F888 sends them to the do-nothing 0xFB22C8) but are IDENTICAL at slots 32 and 33 — so GM System On/Off behave the same on either path.

findings.topic: The unit also TRANSMITS GM System On / GM System Off over MIDI
findings.detail: A six-byte template pair sits in prom_b at 0xF4FEE6 and 0xF4FEEC. sub_FB4CAE picks 0xF4FEE6 (GM System On) when byte +1 of its argument record is 0x11 and 0xF4FEEC (GM System Off) when it is 0x10, then hands the 6 bytes to the SysEx transmit path. The bytes are byte-for-byte the same as the two messages the unit receives.

findings.topic: The same two messages are written into Standard MIDI Files, selected by the GM-mode flag
findings.detail: Three SMF writers each carry an 8-byte pair of SMF track events — delta-time 0x00, then a 5-byte SysEx event — and choose between them at write time. Two of the three choose with `bit 2,(0x7f4d)`, i.e. by the very flag the received GM messages set and clear: bit set -> GM System On is written as the track's first event, bit clear -> GM System Off. The third selects on (0x1239) instead. Only one of the three copies is annotated in the tree; the other two are still emitted as unnamed data blocks with their readers identified but their role not written up.

findings.topic: Trailing bytes before the F7 are probably tolerated
findings.detail: The trie walk stops the instant it matches a record whose action byte is non-zero — for GM that is the sub-ID#2 byte. Nothing afterwards checks the message length, and the dispatch gate is only 'parse-record slot 4 is zero and slot 0 is below 0x22'. So F0 7E 7F 09 01 <extra bytes> F7 would most likely still be taken as GM System On. Marked LIKELY: this follows from the absence of a length check, not from a positive test, and it has not been confirmed on hardware.
findings.symbols: sub_FB63D1 exit .LFB6B6C 0xFB6B6C; dispatch gate in sub_FB225D at 0xFB227A (`cp A,0x00` on slot 4) and 0xFB2291 (`cp A,0x22` on slot 0)

findings.topic: The manufacturer-ID byte is not re-checked after the front end
findings.detail: The front end accepts ID 0x50 or 0x7E, then sub_FB63D1 skips two bytes without looking at either, and the level-1 list is shared by both ID families (it holds the Technics command bytes 0x21-0x2D and 0x7E alongside 0x7F). Consequently F0 50 7F 09 01 F7 would most likely be decoded as GM System On exactly as F0 7E 7F 09 01 F7 is, and conversely F0 7E 21 04 00 11 F7 would enter the Technics command path. Marked LIKELY: it follows from the missing check rather than from an explicit test, and there is no evidence the firmware ever sends such a hybrid.

findings.topic: A global kill switch on SysEx reception: (0x89) == 0xFF
findings.detail: Both drainers open with `cp (0x89),0xff / jrl z, <exit>` and return without touching the rings when the byte at 0x89 is 0xFF. While that holds, no SysEx of any kind — Technics or universal — is processed. What sets (0x89) is not established in this tree; the existing notes list it under 'still not converted'.

findings.topic: Context for the manual: the rest of the SysEx engine is Matsushita ID 0x50
findings.detail: The same trie and the same 34-slot dispatch table serve a Technics/Matsushita command set carried under ID 0x50. The level-1 list admits command bytes 0x21, 0x22, 0x23, 0x24, 0x25, 0x27, 0x28, 0x29, 0x2A, 0x2B, 0x2C, 0x2D and 0x7E. Fixed transmit templates for the short handshake messages sit at 0xF4FEA8-0xF4FF60. WARNING: which company holds MIDI manufacturer ID 0x50 is deliberately NOT asserted anywhere in this tree — it needs the MMA assignment list, which is not present here. Do not print a company name on the strength of the byte.

findings.topic: Provenance note: the task's two named entry points are on the transmit/UI side, not the receive side
findings.detail: GmSystemSysEx_F76E64 is in prom_b (not prom_a as the brief states): it is the Standard-MIDI-File writer's pair of 8-byte track events, i.e. what the unit WRITES INTO A FILE, not what it parses from the wire. Paint_GeneralMidiMode_Entry (prom_a 0xF99844) is a three-byte wrapper around the panel painter Paint_GeneralMidiMode (0xF99D0C) for screen id 0x7A. The receive-side decode is elsewhere entirely — prom_a 0xFB20CE/0xFB21CB and 0xFB63D1, with tables in prom_b at 0xF4FF61/0xF5115B and 0xF4F800/0xF4F888.

openQuestions: What bit 7 of (0x60F020) means. Both GM handlers set it before posting their event, and nothing converted in this tree reads it.

What consumes the {E=0x91, D=0x03, A=<(0x7F4D)>, W=0x04} record on the 0x2E00 pending list. Until that is traced, 'GM System On replaces the current settings with the GM settings' is the panel dialog's claim, not something the disassembly establishes for the SysEx path.

What sets byte +1 of sub_FB4CAE's argument record to 0x11 or 0x10 — i.e. what actually makes the unit TRANSMIT GM System On/Off over MIDI (as opposed to writing it into an SMF). The template selection is proven; the trigger is not.
What (0x89) is and who sets it to 0xFF. While it is 0xFF, both SysEx drainers exit immediately and no SysEx at all is processed.

Whether trailing bytes between the sub-ID#2 and the F7 are genuinely tolerated. Needs a hardware test: send F0 7E 7F 09 01 00 F7 and see whether GM mode turns on. Hardware is currently unreachable — park it in kn7000_mame/notes/HARDWARE-QUESTIONS-PENDING-FELIPE.md rather than asserting it.
Whether F0 50 7F 09 01 F7 really acts as GM System On (the ID byte is never re-checked after the front-end filter). Same hardware test applies.
Which company holds MIDI manufacturer ID 0x50. The tree refuses to name it without the MMA assignment list; the published manual should do the same.
What the Matsushita commands 1-33 do individually. Only the two GM slots were traced here; PtrTable_F4F800 slot 9 (0xFB33FE) and slots 23-31 have distinct handlers that were not read.

Data_F73844 and Data_F75675 (prom_b) are still classified as unidentified data blocks even though they are byte-identical SMF GM-event pairs with located readers. Their headers should be corrected in the disassembly; that is a source edit this pass did not make.

No reproducibility artefact was committed for this pass. The enumeration above was done by reading the .s files plus one throwaway Python byte-scan of original_ROMs/*. If any of these byte sequences are published, a small committed probe (walk LinkTable_F4FF61 from record 767 and print every accepted message) belongs beside the disassembly, per the project's permanent-storage rule.

findings.topic: There are two MIDI input pumps and they differ by ONE byte: the port tag
findings.detail: MIDI messages reach the application through two byte-for-byte twin routines. MidiIn_PumpPortA (0xFA6018) drains ring 0x600C1E; MidiIn_PumpPortB (0xFA60C2) drains ring 0x601028. Each pump calls its own fetch routine, which copies one message into the staging record at 0x1940..0x1943 and writes a constant PORT TAG into (0x1943): MidiIn_FetchMessage_PortA writes 0x00 at 0xFA60A4, MidiIn_FetchMessage_PortB writes 0x10 at 0xFA612D. The two pumps are 97 bytes each and differ in exactly four bytes (ring base and two ring-veneer addresses); the two fetch routines are 0x28 bytes and differ in four (ring base, scan veneer, and the tag byte). Everything downstream of the tag is shared code.

findings.topic: The port tag is bit 4 of a 5-bit channel index: 32 logical channels, 16 per port
findings.detail: MidiIn_RouteChannelMessage builds the routing index as (status & 0x0F) | (0x1943), i.e. channel in bits 0-3 and the port tag in bit 4. That 0..0x1F index selects an entry of the 32-byte offset table at 0x1800, whose value is an offset into the list area at 0x1820 (64 bytes) holding `count, part, part, ...`. So MIDI 1 occupies indices 0x00-0x0F and MIDI 2 indices 0x10-0x1F, and every routing decision in the instrument is made on the combined 5-bit value, never on the port alone.

MidiIn_BuildChannelRouteTable (0xFA6F21) fills exactly that shape: it clears 0x20 bytes at 0x1800 and 0x40 at 0x1820, loops W = 0..0x1F (`cp (0x197A),0x20` at FA7013) and matches each part's byte +0x0D masked with 0x1F (FA6FC8/FA6FD3).

findings.topic: MIDI 1 is CPU 1's own UART; MIDI 2 arrives pre-parsed over the inter-CPU link
findings.detail: Nothing on CPU 1 receives MIDI 2 bytes from a UART. CPU 1's serial channel 0 (SC0) is MIDI 1: its receive ISR MIDI_RX_Byte parses bytes and appends finished messages to ring 0x600C1E, which is exactly the ring MidiIn_PumpPortA reads (tag 0x00). The port-B ring 0x601028 has only TWO writers in either image, both inside the FOREGROUND parser: MIDI_Fg_Deliver2 at 0xFA5AA4 and MIDI_Fg_Deliver3 at 0xFA5ADC, both through Ring601028_PutBlock (0xF41DD4). That foreground parser, MIDI_DrainQueue (0xFA5942), takes its raw bytes from ring 0x60195A (Ring60195A_Get, 0xF41D18), and ring 0x60195A is filled by the INTER-CPU LINK receive path: the link's selector-1 arm indexes an 8-entry table at prom_b 0xF57D4F by the command byte's top three bits, and index 6 is 0xF57C72 = Ring60195A_PutBlock_Ldir. Outbound, port B is not a UART either: MIDI_PostSendWork_PortB (0xFA5C12) empties ring 0x60153C into a stack buffer and hands it to Link_SendBlockIn32ByteChunks (0xF40ED4 -> prom_a 0xF8E02C) with selector 2.

findings.topic: That the far end of the link is the physical MIDI 2 jack is an inference, not a schematic fact
findings.detail: The tree's schematic-derived pin table names CPU 1's TXD0/RXD0 as MIDI1OUT/MIDI1IN and P82 as MIDI1SNS. prom_c (CPU 2) independently implements a complete second MIDI port on ITS serial channel 0 - MIDI range filter, 0xFE active-sensing flag, 31250 baud - and forwards bytes CPU 1 sends on link channel 2 straight to that UART (Link_Ch2_ForwardBytes -> MIDI_Tx_PutByte), while sending its own received bytes to CPU 1 on link channel 6. Channel 2 is the selector CPU 1's port-B transmitters push, and channel 6 is the index whose sink is ring 0x60195A. So port B end-to-end is CPU 2's SC0. What is NOT in this tree is a schematic label calling CPU 2's SC0 'MIDI 2'.

findings.topic: SYSTEM EXCLUSIVE never travels in the port-A/port-B message rings at all
findings.detail: Neither input pump can ever see a SysEx. On the interrupt side, MIDI_RX_SystemCommon sends 0xF0 to MIDI_RX_SysExStart, which forwards the accepted bytes to Ring601646_Put (0xF41E3C) - a different ring from 0x600C1E. On the foreground side, MIDI_Fg_SystemCommon posts the accepted header to Ring601C6E_PutBlock (0xF41EAC) and MIDI_Fg_SysExData posts body bytes to Ring601C6E_Put (0xF41EA8) - again not 0x601028. And even if a 0xF0 did reach a pump, MidiIn_SystemMessage indexes MidiIn_SystemSubTable by the status byte's LOW NIBBLE, so 0xF0 lands on slot 0, which is MidiIn_SystemIgnore (a `or (0x9F),0x01` and RET). Only 0xF2 (slot 2) and 0xF3 (slot 3) have handlers. SysEx is therefore a wholly separate transport on both ports.

findings.topic: Two SysEx identifiers are accepted and only two: 0x50 and 0x7E
findings.detail: Every stage of the SysEx path applies the same two-value test on the byte after 0xF0. A message with any other identifier stays 'armed' (so the parser still tracks where it ends) but is never forwarded. There is NO device-number / unit-number byte tested anywhere in the converted receive path, and none is inserted anywhere in the converted transmit path - the outgoing templates are copied byte-for-byte out of ROM with no masking or ORing.

findings.topic: State bytes: (0xA9) interrupt-side, (0x0964) foreground-side, same bit layout
findings.detail: Both SysEx state machines use bit 0 = 'a SysEx is armed' (set the moment 0xF0 arrives), bit 1 = 'the identifier was accepted', bit 5 = a suppression bit. Body bytes are forwarded only when bit 1 is set AND bit 5 is clear. MIDI_Fg_SystemCommon writes the literal 3 (bits 0+1) on acceptance; MIDI_DrainQueue writes 4 after a clean 0xF7 close and 0 when any other status byte aborts the message.

findings.topic: The two SysEx assemblers are twins, one per port - so ORDINARY SysEx reception is not MIDI-1-only
findings.detail: sub_FB20CE drains ring 0x601646 (the MIDI 1 / interrupt-side SysEx queue) and sub_FB21CB drains ring 0x601C6E (the MIDI 2 / foreground-side queue). They are the same routine: a 3-state machine at (0x60FD43) - state 0 waits for 0xF0, state 1 accepts 0x50 or 0x7E, state 2 takes body bytes - appending through sub_FB6165 and, on 0xF7, running the message processor sub_FB2160. Both are dispatched every pass of the main loop. So a Technics or Universal SysEx arriving on MIDI 2 IS parsed and IS acted on; the MIDI-1-only restriction the manual describes is NOT a property of the general SysEx receiver.

findings.topic: ★ What confines BULK DUMP to MIDI 1: the dump's own send and receive loops name only the MIDI 1 rings
findings.detail: There are two block transmitters in prom_a and they differ ONLY in which ports they write. sub_FB7165 (0xFB7165) splits the frame into 0x20-byte chunks and pushes each through Ring601432_PutBlock (0xF41DF8) + MIDI_PostSendWork (0xF40724) - port A / MIDI 1 ONLY. sub_FB71BB (0xFB71BB) pushes each chunk through BOTH that pair AND Ring60153C_PutBlock (0xF41E1C) + MIDI_PostSendWork_PortB (0xF40730) - both ports. Both prepare the frame with the same helper (0xFB5F65). The BULK DUMP transmit engine sub_FB6F6B / sub_FB6FB2 uses sub_FB7165, i.e. MIDI 1 only; the 14 live-parameter/'MIDI out' senders at 0xFB33EE..0xFB555B use sub_FB71BB, i.e. both ports. Symmetrically, the blocking bulk-dump RECEIVE loop sub_FB6098 reads ring 0x601646 (0xF41E38) and nothing else, and its caller sub_FB6072 first spins until the MIDI 1 OUT ring 0x601432 is empty. Both directions of the bulk dump are therefore hard-wired to MIDI 1 at the call-site level - there is no setting involved.

findings.topic: Ring 0x601432 is MIDI 1 OUT, ring 0x60153C is MIDI 2 OUT, and (0x194B) is the runtime port select
findings.detail: Ring 0x601432 is drained one byte at a time by the INTTX0 handler MIDI_TX_Ready straight into SC0BUF, so it is the MIDI 1 transmit queue. Ring 0x60153C is drained by MIDI_PostSendWork_PortB into the link with selector 2, so it is the MIDI 2 transmit queue. For the staged-message output path the choice is data-driven: MidiOut_PostStagedMessage tests `cp (0x194B),0x00` and takes MIDI_PostSendWork (0xF40724) when zero, MIDI_PostSendWork_PortB (0xF40730) otherwise, with the matching PutBlock chosen ten instructions earlier. MIDI_SendBankAndProgram uses a different, per-call selector: bit 4 of its channel argument - clear sends through Ring601432_PutBlock, set sends through the link - which is the same bit 4 that is the input-side port tag.

findings.topic: Every buffer size, from the ring class itself
findings.detail: All fourteen rings are instances of one class whose control block sits ten bytes below the data pointer: -10 scan cursor, -8 read cursor, -6 scan limit, -4 write cursor, -2 FREE BYTES REMAINING, +0.. data. Init seeds the free count with capacity-1, so one slot of every ring is permanently unused. The MIDI ones are: 0x600C1E = 0x400 (MIDI 1 IN messages, 1023 usable), 0x601028 = 0x400 (MIDI 2 IN messages, 1023), 0x601646 = 0x200 (MIDI 1 SysEx bytes, 511), 0x601C6E = 0x200 (MIDI 2 SysEx bytes, 511), 0x60195A = 0x200 (MIDI 2 raw byte stream from the link, 511), 0x601432 = 0x100 (MIDI 1 OUT, 255), 0x60153C = 0x100 (MIDI 2 OUT, 255). On the CPU 2 side the queues are a 22-byte descriptor pair: RX 0x00F2FB over 0x7EDA-0x82D9 (1024 bytes, free 0x03FF) and TX 0x00F311 over 0x82DA-0x84D9 (512 bytes, free 0x01FF).

findings.topic: Input overrun: four distinct failure modes, three counters, one flush
findings.detail: (1) A byte that arrives with a UART error never reaches the parser: MIDI_RX_ErrorReset reads SC0BUF to clear the condition, drops running status, sets (0x9E) bit 3 and increments the 8-BIT counter at (0x0931). (2) A message that will not fit is dropped whole and sets (0x9E) bit 2 plus the 8-bit counter at (0x0932) - the free-space tests are `cp (XIX+0xFE),0x0003` before writing 2 bytes and `,0x0004` before writing 3, one more than is about to be written. (3) CONGESTION SHEDDING: before the ordinary test, if free space is 0x40 or less and the message is a Note On (`and D,0xF0 / cp D,0x90`) with NON-ZERO velocity, it is thrown away; a Note On with velocity 0 - a release under running status - falls through and is delivered. So an overloaded input loses note starts and never loses note ends. (4) Recovery: the main loop tests `(0x9E) & 0x2C` (bits 2, 3, 5) and, if any is set, calls Ring600C1E_Init (0xF41DB8) - the entire MIDI 1 input ring is discarded - then clears those bits with `and (0x9E),0xD3`.

findings.topic: Output overrun: 240 polls, then the whole transmit queue is thrown away
findings.detail: MidiOut_PostStagedMessage will not enqueue unless the selected port's ring has at least 3 free bytes. It polls, counting (0xA2) from 0 up to 0xF0 = 240, reading the free-count cell directly (0x601430 for port A, 0x60153A for port B). On timeout it writes 0xF6 to SC0BUF and calls the port's ring Init - Ring601432_Init (0xF41E00) for port A, Ring60153C_Init (0xF41E24) for port B - so everything queued for that port is discarded. It also sets (0x9E) bit 0.

findings.topic: SysEx accumulation has its own 255-byte ceiling
findings.detail: Incoming SysEx bytes are appended by sub_FB6165 into the buffer named by the descriptor pointer at (0x60FC80): the byte is stored at *(desc+0x0A)++, a 0xFF sentinel is written after it, and the 16-bit counter at desc+0x00 is incremented - except on 0xF0, which RESETS the counter to 1. Before appending a data byte the assemblers read that counter and compare it with 0x00FF; at 255 or more the message is aborted. sub_FB20CE and sub_FB21CB abandon silently (state back to 0, then sub_FB80F3); the bulk-dump receive loop sub_FB6098 instead raises status code 6 through sub_FB6219 and stops.

findings.topic: ★ The bulk-dump packet format, read out of the transmit engine
findings.detail: A bulk-dump item is set up by appending a 12-byte header template from ROM (sub_FB6E7F), then sub_FB6F6B loops: sub_FB7040 NIBBLISES the source data - each source byte becomes two bytes, HIGH nibble first, `(b>>4)` then `(b & 0x0F)` - and keeps going while the frame's byte count is below 0xFC = 252; sub_FB70AE appends a one-byte CONTINUATION FLAG, 1 if the remaining-length counter (0x60FD00) is non-zero and 0 if the transfer is finished; sub_FB7111 appends the CHECKSUM and the terminating 0xF7. The checksum is an 8-bit sum of the frame from offset +0x0F (the byte after 0xF0) up to but not including the checksum, negated, with bit 7 cleared: `(-sum) & 0x7F`. The 0xF7 is not computed - it is byte 1 of the 16-bit constant at 0xF4FE68, whose bytes are 00 F7, loaded before the low byte is overwritten with the checksum. Only then does sub_FB7165 push the frame to MIDI 1.

findings.topic: ★ The bulk-dump address and length fields are 3 bytes of base-128, MSB first - proved by a tiling check and by two measured region sizes

findings.topic: The received-SysEx command dispatch: a 34-entry table at prom_b 0xF4F800
findings.detail: When a SysEx closes with 0xF7, sub_FB2160 reads two fields out of a 16-byte record through the byte-accessor sub_FB62D3(record, index): field 4 must be 0, and field 0 must be below 0x22. Field 0 is then multiplied by 4, added to 0x00F4F800 and the resulting LE32 pointer is entered with a stack-argument tail jump. So the machine recognises 34 SysEx commands, numbered 0x00-0x21. sub_FB62D3 is a 16-way jump table that simply returns record[index]; its write twin sub_FB6219 is the same table storing a byte.

The 16-entry bound on both accessors is the ROM's own (`cp BC,0x000F / jrl ugt` at FB622C and FB62E2) and each has the tree's last-entry test in its header. ⚠ Which WIRE bytes land in record fields 0 and 4 is NOT established here - sub_FB63AF, which fills the record, was not traced.

findings.topic: The MIDI settings that touch SysEx: an EXCLUSIVE filter, and no device number
findings.detail: The MIDI INPUT&OUTPUT FILTER screen has eight ON/OFF fields, each a bit-field in the 0x7F30 block. In screen order they are PROGRAM CHANGE = (0x7F39) bit 4, BANK SELECT = (0x7F3A) bit 7, PITCH BEND = (0x7F39) bit 6, CONTROL CHANGE = (0x7F39) bit 3, RESET ALL CTRL = (0x7F3B) bit 0, CHANNEL PRESSURE = (0x7F39) bit 5, SONG SELECT = (0x7F33) bit 3, EXCLUSIVE = (0x7F38) bits 0-3 (displayed ON when the nibble is non-zero). A byte-level census over all four ROMs finds exactly six references to 0x7F38: three are this screen, and the other three - 0xFB3398, 0xFB341E, 0xFB4B7F - all test `and C,0x08`, i.e. bit 3, as a gate on sending a live-parameter SysEx. No reference to 0x7F38 exists in any receive path, and none exists in prom_b, prom_c or prom_d at all. There is no MIDI channel or device-number setting anywhere in the SysEx path: the channel settings - MIDI INPUT MODE (0x7F35) low nibble, SINGLE CHANNEL (0x7F36) & 0x1F - are consumed only by MidiIn_BuildChannelRouteTable for channel-voice routing.

openQuestions: The manual's 'BULK DUMP only on MIDI 1' is explained by call sites, not by a setting: sub_FB7165 (send) names only ring 0x601432 and sub_FB6098 (receive) names only ring 0x601646. But ORDINARY SysEx reception exists on both ports (sub_FB21CB drains the MIDI 2 SysEx ring 0x601C6E every main-loop pass). If the manual also says non-bulk SysEx is MIDI-1-only, that is NOT what the firmware does and the manual text should be checked before publication.

Which company holds manufacturer ID 0x50 is not settled in this tree, and the tree contradicts itself: the header at prom_a 0xFA5AEB says 'Matsushita', notes/FINDINGS-midi-port.md explicitly refuses to name one. Needs the MMA assignment list.

That CPU 2's serial channel 0 is the physical MIDI 2 jack is an inference from the link-channel wiring (link selector 2 = CPU1->CPU2 MIDI bytes, link index 6 = CPU2->CPU1 MIDI bytes). The schematic pin table in notes/DRIVER-INSIGHT-wsa1-2026-09-02.md names only MIDI1OUT/MIDI1IN/MIDI1SNS, and that table has already needed one off-by-one correction. A MIDI2 pin label from the service manual would close it.

sub_FB63AF, which builds the 16-byte record that sub_FB2160 dispatches on, was not traced, so the mapping from wire bytes to record fields 0 and 4 is unknown. Until that is done, 'command number = record[0], 0x00-0x21' cannot be turned into 'the byte at wire offset N is the command'. The 34-entry table at prom_b 0xF4F800 is the next thing to enumerate for the manual.

Frame-length arithmetic is one byte from a contradiction and should be measured, not reasoned about: the transmitter stops adding nibble pairs once the frame reaches 0xFC = 252 bytes and then appends flag + checksum + F7, while the receiver aborts a message whose accumulated count reaches 0xFF = 255. Whether the largest frame the machine emits is 255 or 256 bytes - and therefore whether it can overrun its own receiver - needs the reset point of the count at (0x60FC88)+0 (sub_FB7BB9 / sub_FB8081) to be read.

The EXCLUSIVE field is edited with bit mask 0x0F but the transmit gates test only bit 3. The reading that ON writes all four bits (0x0F) and OFF writes 0x00 is consistent with both, but the bit-field setter at 0xFB... reached by `calr 0xf22b` from 0xF9AF37 was not read, so it is inference. Do not publish 'EXCLUSIVE = (0x7F38) bit 3' as the storage format without reading that setter.

sub_FB7025 conditionally prepends the 3-byte fragment F0 50 7E when (0x60FCE4)+0x0F == 1, inside the same per-packet loop that already has a 12-byte header in the buffer. Whether that is the continuation-packet header (and therefore whether packets 2..n look different from packet 1 on the wire) is not established.

Reproducibility: the four-ROM address census quoted in the settings finding was run ad hoc as `python3` over original_ROMs/*, scanning the 12 TLCS-900 direct-memory prefix spellings (0xC1/D1/E1/F1 with a 16-bit address field, 0xC2/D2/E2/F2 with a 24-bit one) for 0x7F32/33/35/36/38/39/3A/3B. notes/prom_a_xref.py and notes/prom_c_xrefs.py already do this properly for their own images; the cross-image sweep should be added to one of them and committed rather than left in scratch.

findings.topic: How F0 reaches the SysEx handler at all
findings.detail: 0xF0 arrives as an ordinary status byte in MIDI_RX_Byte and is only stored as running status in (0x9A); nothing SysEx-specific happens yet. The SysEx handler runs when the NEXT byte arrives: it has bit 7 clear, so MIDI_RX_DataByte takes it, finds (0xA9) bit 0 still clear, forms (running_status & 0x70) >> 2 and jumps through MIDI_StatusDispatch_Table slot 7 to MIDI_RX_SystemCommon, which compares D against 0xF0 and branches to MIDI_RX_SysExStart with D = 0xF0 and E = that byte. So the byte the acceptance test looks at is the FIRST DATA BYTE after F0, i.e. message byte index 1.

findings.topic: The identifier test — exactly two bytes, both fixed immediates
findings.detail: MIDI_RX_SysExStart first writes (0xA9) = 0x01 ("armed") for EVERY F0, then tests the identifier byte against two literal immediates: 0x50 and 0x7E. Either one takes the Accept path. There is no third comparison, no table lookup and no read of any setting or NVRAM cell on this path — both values are immediate operands of `cp E,imm8`. 0x7E is MIDI's Universal Non-Real Time ID. There is NO device/unit number or model ID compared at this level; the very next byte is already treated as body data.

findings.topic: What makes it take the Ignore path, and what Ignore actually does
findings.detail: MIDI_SysEx_Ignore (0xFA586D) is nothing but the shared `ret` — it is also the fall-through of Accept. Taking it means: (0xA9) keeps the value 0x01, i.e. ARMED but NOT accepted. The consequence is deliberate: every following data byte still reaches MIDI_RX_SysExData (because bit 0 is set) and is dropped there (because bit 1 is clear), so the unit tracks another maker's message to its F7 without acting on it. Ignore is taken for any identifier byte that is neither 0x50 nor 0x7E.

findings.topic: Termination and the abort rule — how a message ends
findings.detail: Termination is handled back in MIDI_RX_Byte's status-byte arm, not in the SysEx routines. With (0xA9) bit 0 set: if bit 1 is CLEAR (an ignored maker), any status byte ends the message quietly — (0x9A)=0 and (0xA9) &= 0xCC, clearing bits 0,1,4,5. If bit 1 is SET: a 0xF7 with bit 5 clear forwards the 0xF7 itself through 0xF41E3C and then writes (0xA9)=0x04, which the following `and 0xCC` preserves — so 0x04 is the "a complete SysEx was received" residue. Any OTHER status byte 0x80..0xF6 aborts: (0xA9)=0x10, (0x9A)=0, and nothing is forwarded. System Real Time 0xF8..0xFF never reaches this arm (it is split off at 0xFA54B6), so a clock or active-sensing byte inside a SysEx does NOT break it — correct MIDI 1.0 behaviour.

findings.topic: Where received data is buffered, and exactly what bounds it
findings.detail: Neither ring is the message buffer. Two near-identical collectors drain them — sub_FB20CE from ring 0x601646 (interrupt side, via 0xF41E38) and sub_FB21CB from ring 0x601C6E (foreground side, via 0xF41EA4) — and both append into the SAME message buffer through sub_FB6165, sharing one state byte at (0x60FD43): 0 = waiting for F0, 1 = waiting for the identifier, 2 = body. sub_FB6165 stores the byte at the cursor desc[+0x0A], post-increments it, writes a 0xFF sentinel one past it, and maintains a 16-bit count at desc[+0x00]: an F0 RESETS the count to 1, every other byte increments it. THE BOUND: a body data byte is appended only while that count is below 0x00FF — `cp WA,0x00ff / jr nc` rejects at 255 and resets the collector. The identifier byte and the closing 0xF7 bypass that test, so the longest message that can be stored is F0 + identifier + 253 data bytes + F7 = 256 bytes, plus the sentinel.

findings.detail: sub_FB7F42 installs four buffer descriptors: (0x60FC80)=0x60F820 (the active one), (0x60FC84)=0x60F938, (0x60FC88)=0x60FA50, (0x60FC8C)=0x60FB68. sub_FB7FEB resets a descriptor: count desc[+0x00]=0, and the three cursors desc[+0x02] (read), desc[+0x06] and desc[+0x0A] (write) all set to desc+0x0E, with a 0xFF sentinel written there. So payload starts 14 bytes into each descriptor. The four are spaced 0x118 apart and the last one ends exactly at 0x60FC80 where the pointer table begins, which makes the payload area 0x118-0x0E = 0x10A = 266 bytes each — comfortably above the 257 bytes the count bound allows. sub_FB8028 swaps the active and alternate descriptors, so this is a double buffer.

findings.topic: ★ The grammar walker SKIPS F0 and the identifier without re-comparing them
findings.detail: sub_FB63D1 begins by adding 2 to the buffer's read cursor and then reading one byte — so the first byte it examines is message byte index 2. Bytes 0 (F0) and 1 (the manufacturer/Universal identifier) are never compared again, and the identifier is never stored into the parse record. Consequence for a manual: the command grammar below is reachable with EITHER identifier — e.g. `F0 7E 21 04 00 11 F7` parses exactly like `F0 50 21 04 00 11 F7`, and `F0 50 7F 09 01 F7` parses as GM System On. Whether an individual handler re-reads the raw buffer to check byte 1 was not found, but no such read was located.

findings.topic: ★ The accepted third byte — the root table, 14 values
findings.detail: The walker matches message byte 2 against a 6-byte-record table at prom_b 0xF5115B, bounded to 15 records (the 15th is the 0xFF terminator). Record layout = [0] match byte, [1] command id (0 means descend), [2..5] LE32 pointer to the next node. The 14 accepted values, in table order, are: 0x25, 0x7E, 0x23, 0x24, 0x2D, 0x27, 0x28, 0x2C, 0x2B, 0x7F, 0x29, 0x2A, 0x21, 0x22. Note 0x26 is NOT accepted. Two of them terminate immediately: 0x25 yields command 0x09 and 0x7E yields command 0x0A with no further bytes matched.

findings.topic: ★ The complete short-form accepted sequences, with their command numbers
findings.detail: Walking the trie gives, for the sequences that terminate within a few bytes: `F0 .. 23 7E F7` = cmd 0x01; `24 7E` = 0x02; `27 7E` = 0x03; `28 7E` = 0x04; `29 7E` = 0x05; `2A 7E` = 0x04 (same command as 0x28); `25` = 0x09; `7E` = 0x0A; `21 04 <00|01> 11` = 0x07; `22 04 <00|01> 11` = 0x08; `7F 09 01` = 0x20 (this is MIDI's standard GM System On); `7F 09 02` = 0x21 (GM System Off). findings.topic: ★ The byte after 0x04 is a two-valued unit/device field; 04 nn 11 is a model triple
findings.detail: In every 0x21 / 0x22 / 0x2B / 0x2C / 0x2D family the grammar demands 0x04, then EITHER 0x00 OR 0x01, then 0x11. Both values are literal match bytes in separate records (e.g. node 0xF4FF73 holds `00 00 <ptr>` and `01 00 <ptr>`, both pointing at node 0xF4FF67 which matches 0x11) — they are NOT read from a setting, a DIP strap or NVRAM at match time. The matched bytes are stored into the parse record at indices 6, 7 and 8. sub_FB2323 transmits F0 50 21 04 00 11 F7 up to three times, waits for command 0x08 (which is `F0 .. 22 04 <00|01> 11`), and then COPIES parse-record fields 6, 7 and 8 into (0x60FC90), (0x60FC91) and (0x60FC92) — i.e. it remembers the responding unit's triple. Those three cells are written there and initialised to 0xFF by sub_FB7F1F, but no reader of them was found anywhere in prom_a.

findings.topic: Validation: the parse record, its error codes, and the dispatch bound
findings.detail: The walk fills a 16-byte parse record whose pointer is (0x60FCD8)=0x60FC98, initialised from a ROM template at prom_b 0xF511E9 = `00 00 00 00 00 FF FF FF FF FF FF FF FF FF FF FF`. Field 0 = the command id, field 4 = an error code (0 = OK), fields 5..0x0E = the matched message bytes from index 2 onwards. A miss in the ROOT table writes error 0x07; a miss in any deeper node writes 0x08; the deepest loop writes 0x10. After the walk, sub_FB2160 (interrupt-side) and sub_FB225D (foreground) require field 4 == 0, then require field 0 < 0x22, then dispatch through a 34-entry LE32 handler table — 0xF4F800 for the interrupt-side ring and 0xF4F888 for the foreground ring. The two tables TILE (0xF4F800 + 34*4 = 0xF4F888), which is the last-entry test on the count. The two differ only in their default slot: unhandled commands run 0xFB2820 (a bulk-transfer session loop) on the interrupt side and 0xFB22C8 (reset and return, a no-op) on the foreground side.

findings.topic: A third, stricter collector accepts ONLY 0x50
findings.detail: sub_FB6098 is a blocking receiver that drains the interrupt-side ring 0x601646 itself, with its own local state. Unlike the two background collectors it accepts ONLY 0x50 as the identifier — there is no 0x7E test. It reports through parse-record field 4: 1 = first byte was not F0, 2 = identifier was not 0x50, 3 = a status byte other than F7 arrived mid-message, 6 = the 0xFF byte-count bound was hit. On any of errors 1/2/3 (but not 6) it also sets (0xA9) bit 5, which is what suppresses further SysEx forwarding in the interrupt parser until the next F0. On a clean F7 it sets bit 5 of (0x60FD40).

openQuestions: Who reads (0xA9) bits 2 and 4? They are written (0x04 after a clean F7, 0x10 after an aborted SysEx) but a census of every (0xA9) site in prom_a finds no test of either. If nothing reads them they are diagnostics only — but a reader could live in prom_c/prom_d, which were not searched.

Do the command HANDLERS re-check the manufacturer byte? The grammar walker provably skips message bytes 0 and 1, so at the grammar level `F0 7E 21 04 00 11 F7` is accepted identically to `F0 50 21 ...`. Many handlers do re-read the raw buffer descriptor (0x60FC80), so a late check is possible; none was located. This must be settled before a manual states that either identifier works.

The tables contain command ids up to 0x27, but both dispatchers reject anything >= 0x22. Commands 0x22-0x27 therefore parse successfully and are then dropped by sub_FB2160/sub_FB225D. Is there a third dispatcher with a larger bound, or are those table entries dead? Only one site each references 0xF4F800 and 0xF4F888.

What do commands 0x01-0x1F actually do? On the interrupt-side ring, 0x01-0x08 and 0x0A-0x16 all land on the single shared handler 0xFB2820, which gates on the panel-mode cell (0x207A)==0x79 and on command >= 7; on the foreground ring the same commands land on a no-op. Distinct handlers exist only for 0x00, 0x09, 0x17, 0x18, 0x19, 0x1A, 0x1B-0x1F, 0x20, 0x21.

The 0x2B / 0x2C / 0x2D subtrees (338 reachable nodes) are the bulk of the protocol — parameter addresses after `04 <00|01> 11` — and were not enumerated. The committed probe dumps them with --paths; they need a pass of their own before any parameter table goes into a manual.

What is the unit byte after 0x04 for — a device number selectable in the UI, or a MAIN/SUB distinction between two linked units? The grammar accepts 0x00 and 0x01 unconditionally and the value is only remembered (0x60FC91), never compared. Felipe's hardware could settle this by watching what the instrument sends for its own unit.

The 266-byte payload capacity per buffer is arithmetic on the 0x118 descriptor stride and the abutment at 0x60FC80, not a constant in the ROM. Worth confirming against a MAME memory map before it is printed as a limit; the byte-count bound of 255/256 bytes per message IS a ROM constant and is the number a manual should quote.
(0x0964) = 4, set by the foreground parser after a clean F7, has no located reader — the same open question the existing block header at 0xFA5942 already flags.

findings.topic: The whole chain: status byte → message id → screen
findings.detail: None of the three errors is raised as the number 40/41/42. The SysEx engine keeps a parse record whose pointer is RAM (0x60FCD8); field 4 of that record is a STATUS byte. At the end of a bulk-dump session sub_FB7DFE reads it: 0x00 → message 0x23 ("COMPLETED!"); 0x21 → screen 0xB3 with no popup at all; anything else → message := STATUS_MAP[status], where STATUS_MAP is the byte table at prom_b 0xF511C7. The message id is written to RAM (0x2880) and screen request 0xAB is posted. sub_F99098 then paints (0x2880): base = *(0xF993B9 + 4*(0x7FC1)), start = *(base + 8*code), end = *(base + 8*code + 4), handed to display-list interpreter A. Message 0x22 = ERROR 40, 0x21 = ERROR 41, 0x20 = ERROR 42, 0x23 = COMPLETED!. Field accessors: sub_FB6219 sets a field, sub_FB62D3 gets one, both 16-way jump tables over record offsets +0..+15.

findings.topic: ERROR 40 — exact condition
findings.detail: ERROR 40 is message 0x22, and STATUS_MAP maps exactly three statuses to it: 0x08, 0x09 and 0x0A. Those three are raised by the SysEx header parser sub_FB63D1, which matches the incoming message against a 10-level trie in prom_b whose root is 0xF5115B. The parser first advances the buffer read cursor by TWO — the 0xF0 and the manufacturer byte are skipped and never re-compared — so trie depth 1 is message byte [2], depth 2 is byte [3], and so on. Code 0x08 = byte[3] not in the depth-2 node; 0x09 = byte[4] not in the depth-3 node; 0x0A = byte[5] not in the depth-4 node. For every Technics product id the machine knows (0x21, 0x22, 0x2B, 0x2C, 0x2D) the accepted depth-2/3/4 bytes are 0x04, then 0x00 or 0x01, then 0x11 — so for a message addressed to the WSA1 (id 0x2D) ERROR 40 means byte[3] != 0x04, or byte[4] not in {0x00,0x01}, or byte[5] != 0x11. For the six short forms (ids 0x23,0x24,0x27,0x28,0x29,0x2A) depth 2 must be 0x7E. For 0x7F (universal) depth 2 must be 0x09. NOTE that a wrong PRODUCT ID at byte[2] does NOT give ERROR 40 — it gives status 0x07, i.e. ERROR 41.

findings.topic: ERROR 42 — exact condition, and it is a SEND-side error only
findings.detail: ERROR 42 is message 0x20. Three statuses map to it — 0x18, 0x1F and 0x20 — but only 0x20 is ever raised anywhere in the four ROM images. Its single raise is in sub_FB6FB2, the loop that streams a bulk dump OUT: each pass calls Link_WaitBlockDone through prom_b thunk 0xF4123C and, if it returns WA = 0xFFFF, writes status 0x20 to BOTH parse records (*(0x60FCE0) at 0xFB6FFB and *(0x60FCD8) at 0xFB700A). Link_WaitBlockDone returns 0xFFFF when bit 7 of (0x8A) — "a link block transfer is outstanding" — is still set 500 ticks of the free-running counter (0x80) after entry, i.e. about 1.02 s at the 488.28 Hz derived for timer 1; it then also aborts the transfer (DMA3V=0, (0x6007DA)=0, P7 bit 1 set) and bumps the error counter at (0x6007E1). So ERROR 42 is NOT a MIDI handshake failure with the receiving device, despite the on-screen wording: it is the CPU1↔CPU2 block link failing to complete while the dump is being sent.

findings.topic: The checksum, and the three-byte tail every accepted message must have
findings.detail: sub_FB6CFC walks the nibble-encoded body two bytes at a time from the point the trie stopped and must land exactly on (write_ptr - 3); overshooting by one raises status 0x11. That leaves the last three bytes of the message as <flag> <checksum> <F7>. sub_FB6DBD then (a) requires the parse record's field 5 — the product id the trie matched — to be one of 0x7E, 0x2B, 0x2C, 0x2D, otherwise it performs NO checksum check at all; (b) reads <flag>, which must be 0x00 or 0x01 else status 0x12, and stores it in field 15; (c) sums the message bytes from offset 1 (the 0x50 manufacturer id) through <flag> inclusive, computes (-sum) & 0x7F, and compares it with <checksum>; a mismatch is status 0x14 → ERROR 41. The 0xF0 and the trailing 0xF7 are OUTSIDE the sum. Equivalently: (sum of bytes[1..n] + checksum) & 0x7F == 0.

findings.topic: Body encoding: two 7-bit bytes per data byte, high nibble first
findings.detail: The bulk-dump payload is nibble-encoded. On receive, 0xFB72C9-0xFB7301 reads two successive body bytes and forms byte = ((first & 0x0F) << 4) | (second & 0x0F). On transmit, sub_FB7040 does the inverse: `srl c,0x04` gives the first emitted byte and `and (XIX+0x01),0x0f` the second. This is why an odd body length is a hard error (status 0x11).
findings.symbols: receive join 0xFB72E2 `sll h,0x04` + 0xFB72FC `and A,0x0f` + 0xFB7301 `xor L,H`; transmit split sub_FB7040 0xFB7040, 0xFB706F / 0xFB7074
findings.evidence: Instruction sequence read directly at both sites; the two are exact inverses, which is the cross-check.

findings.topic: ⚠ Status 0x16 is NOT one of the 4x errors — it shows ERROR 21! "Memory full"
findings.detail: STATUS_MAP[0x16] is 0x0F, and message 0x0F is the display list at 0xF2DD4F-0xF2DD6B, which reads "ERROR 21!" / "Memory full". It is raised in the receive decoder when the body still has bytes left but the destination counter (0x60FD20) has reached zero — i.e. the incoming dump is larger than the target area. A manual that assumes every SysEx bulk-dump failure is 40/41/42 would get this one wrong.

findings.topic: The three errors are reported ONLY by the SYSEX BULK DUMP screen
findings.detail: Status bytes are written whenever a complete F0…F7 message is parsed, from either MIDI ring, but the popup only appears where sub_FB7DFE runs, and that has exactly two call sites: 0xFB20BF, the tail of the bulk-dump mode dispatcher (gated on bit 7 of (0x60F802)), and 0xFB286F, the tail of the send loop. So a foreign SysEx arriving while the machine is on any other screen sets no visible error. A corollary worth stating carefully: while a bulk-dump session IS open, unrelated SysEx traffic on the MIDI input can set the status and therefore colour the popup that the session ends with.

findings.topic: The messages the machine accepts at all, and the WSA1's own product id
findings.detail: The root table lists 14 product/id bytes plus the 0xFF terminator: 0x21, 0x22, 0x23, 0x24, 0x25, 0x27, 0x28, 0x29, 0x2A, 0x2B, 0x2C, 0x2D, 0x7E, 0x7F. The WSA1's own is 0x2D — every outgoing bulk-dump header template in prom_b begins F0 50 2D 04 00 11. 0x2B and 0x2C carry huge parameter sub-trees (3756 accepted sequences each) while 0x2D carries 16 sequences ending in internal command ids 0x0B, 0x0C, 0x0E and 0x12-0x16. 0x7F 09 01 / 0x7F 09 02, reached as F0 7E 7F 09 01 F7 and F0 7E 7F 09 02 F7, are GM System On and GM System Off (commands 0x20 and 0x21) and prom_b holds both as literals. A matched sequence yields a command id that is bounded by `cp A,0x22` and used to index one of two 34-entry handler tables, 0xF4F800 for a message that came in on the interrupt-side ring and 0xF4F888 for the foreground ring.

findings.topic: Before the trie: the session framer's own three checks
findings.detail: Inside a bulk-dump session the byte-level framer is sub_FB6098 (reached via sub_FB6072). It is a three-state machine on the incoming ring: state 0 accepts only 0xF0 (else status 0x01), state 1 accepts only 0x50 (else status 0x02), state 2 accepts data bytes until 0xF7 — any other status byte gives status 0x03 and also sets bit 5 of (0xA9), and a message longer than 254 bytes gives status 0x06. Outside a session the interrupt-side framers sub_FB20CE / sub_FB21CB accept 0x50 OR 0x7E as the identifier and silently DROP anything else without raising a status at all, which is how another maker's SysEx passes through unremarked.

findings.evidence: 0xFB60E0 `cp H,0xf0`, 0xFB60EE `cp H,0x50`, 0xFB612C `cp H,0xf7`, 0xFB610A `cp WA,0x00ff`. In sub_FB21CB, 0xFB220B `cp H,0x50` / 0xFB2210 `cp H,0x7e` / `jr nz,.LFB2250` where .LFB2250 only resets the state and continues. findings.topic: What the screens actually say, verbatim
findings.detail: ERROR 40! / "The Identification (ID) code of the" / "System Exclusive data received by" / "the WSA is different product."  —  ERROR 41! / "An error has occured during System" / "Exclusive data reception.The data" / "from the transmitting device may be" / "incomplete." / "Please try again."  —  ERROR 42! / "An error has occured during System" / "Exclusive transmition.The data has" / "not been received correctly." / "Please try again."  The firmware's own spellings ("occured", "transmition") are reproduced as-is. Note sub_F99021 also writes 0xFF to (0x209A) for every message id except 0x23 and 0x2C, which is what distinguishes an alert from a plain notice.

openQuestions: The wording of ERROR 42 ("The data has not been received correctly") implies a handshake with the receiving MIDI device, but the only raise is a CPU1↔CPU2 link-block timeout (Link_WaitBlockDone). The tree's own header for Link_WaitBlockDone says of this very call site: "0xFB6FD1 … what it waits on is NOT established". So whether the link block being waited on carries the outgoing MIDI stream to CPU 2 (which would make the manual's wording loosely right) or something else is UNVERIFIED. Do not assert a cause-and-effect with the receiving instrument in the manual.

Semantically odd but repeatedly confirmed: an unknown PRODUCT ID at message byte [2] gives status 0x07 → ERROR 41, while a wrong byte at [3], [4] or [5] gives ERROR 40. If a real-hardware check is ever possible, sending F0 50 99 04 00 11 … (bogus product) vs F0 50 2D 99 00 11 … (good product, bogus next byte) would distinguish 41 from 40 on the panel and settle it. Felipe's hardware is currently unreachable; park it.

Trie depth 3 accepts 0x00 or 0x01 for every product id and both lead to the identical subtree. Reading this as a device/unit number is an INFERENCE (likely); the ROM only says the two values are accepted and equivalent.

The tail flag byte before the checksum must be 0x00 or 0x01 (status 0x12 otherwise) and is stored in field 15 of the parse record. What it MEANS is not established — nothing converted reads field 15 back.

Statuses 0x19-0x1E each guard one bulk-dump section (their guard is `field 3 of *(0x60FCDC) == 0`, i.e. the previous section completed). Which section is which — SOUND, COMBINATION, SYSTEM/PART & MIDI, TOTAL KEYBOARD, per the menu text in Paint_SysexBulkDump — is NOT established and should not be guessed in the manual.

PtrTable_F98DE5 (the German screen set) has no located reader; the tree's own header says so. Whether some other firmware variant of the WSA1R selects it, or it is dead weight from a shared source tree, is unknown.

It re-derives every number quoted above from original_ROMs/, asserts both load bases and prints OK. The pre-existing wsa1/notes/sysex-probes/sysex_grammar_dump.py (0ac8f694) covers the trie. Nothing from this session lives only in scratch.

findings.topic: Data message frame layout
findings.detail: A bulk-dump data frame is: F0 50 2D 04 <dev> 11 <A1 A2 A3> <S1 S2 S3> <nibble data ...> <cont> <sum> F7. 0x50 is the manufacturer id, 0x2D the bulk-data command, 0x04 and 0x11 are fixed bytes present in every 21/22/2B/2C/2D message, <dev> is a unit number that the firmware always TRANSMITS as 0x00 and ACCEPTS as 0x00 or 0x01. A1A2A3 is a 21-bit address as three MSB-first septets, S1S2S3 the transfer size in SOURCE bytes as three MSB-first septets. <cont> is 0x01 when more frames follow and 0x00 on the last frame of the transfer. <sum> is the checksum, then 0xF7.

findings.evidence: The nine headers are literal byte runs in prom_b, each named by exactly one `lda xbc,(imm24)` in prom_a. The receive grammar (trie root prom_b 0xF5115B, walked by sysex_grammar_dump.py) accepts exactly the same byte strings, including both 0x00 and 0x01 in the <dev> position: level tables 0xF5021F (0x04), 0xF5020D (0x00|0x01), 0xF50201 (0x11), 0xF501DD (0x40|0x20|0x50|0x60|0x62).

findings.topic: The address and size fields — proved, not assumed
findings.detail: A1A2A3 and S1S2S3 are each a 21-bit value packed MSB-first into three 7-bit groups, value = (b0<<14)|(b1<<7)|b2. The size counts SOURCE bytes, not transmitted nibbles. Decoded: SYSTEM,PART & MIDI part 1 addr 0x100000 size 0x20; part 2 addr 0x100020 size 0x960; SOUND addr 0x080000 size 0x40000; SEQUENCER part 1 addr 0x180000 size 0xC00; part 2 addr 0x180C00 size 0x7800; part 3 addr 0x188400 size supplied at run time; COMBINATION part 1 addr 0x140000 size 0x300; part 2 addr 0x140300 size 0x16000.

findings.evidence: Four independent agreements, all asserted by wsa1/notes/sysex-probes/sysex_bulkdump_tx.py. (1) Each septet size equals the byte extent the matching prom_a descriptor-writer stores (end-start==size), times the block count where the source is streamed (SOUND 32 x 0x2000, COMBINATION part 2 16 x 0x1600; the loop counts are the literals `ldb h,0x1f` at 0xFB2524 and `ldb h,0x0f` at 0xFB271F, each one pass short because a further block follows the loop). (2) For every category sent in parts, addr(part N+1) - addr(part N) == size(part N): 0x100020-0x100000==0x20, 0x140300-0x140000==0x300, 0x180C00-0x180000==0xC00, 0x188400-0x180C00==0x7800. findings.topic: Data bytes are sent as nibble pairs, high nibble first
findings.detail: Every source byte becomes two message bytes: (byte >> 4) then (byte & 0x0F). So a frame carries exactly half as many source bytes as it has data bytes, and a dump on the wire is twice the size the S1S2S3 field states.

findings.topic: Checksum: (0 - sum) & 0x7F over everything after the leading F0
findings.detail: The checksum byte is (0 - S) & 0x7F where S is the 8-bit sum of every message byte from the SECOND byte (the 0x50 manufacturer id) through the continuation-flag byte inclusive. The leading 0xF0 is NOT summed; the checksum byte itself and the trailing 0xF7 are not summed. Equivalently, (sum of all bytes after F0, including the checksum) mod 128 == 0. The checksum byte and the 0xF7 are appended together from the 2-byte literal at prom_b 0xF4FE68 = 00 F7, with the low byte overwritten by the computed value.
findings.symbols: sub_FB7111 0xFB7111, literal prom_b 0xF4FE68
findings.evidence: 0xFB7119 `ld bc,(0xF4FE68)` then 0xFB7151 `ld (xiz-6),a` overwrites its low byte; 0xFB7121-0xFB7126 `ld xix,(0x60FC88) / add XIX,0x0000000F` starts the sum at buffer offset +0x0F while the message's first byte lives at +0x0E; 0xFB7131 `ld XIY,(XWA+0x0A)` is the write cursor, which points one past the last appended byte; 0xFB7137-0xFB7144 is the byte loop `ld C,(XIX) / add H,C`; 0xFB7146-0xFB714E `ld C,H / extz BC / sub WA,WA / sub WA,BC / res 0x07,A`; 0xFB7154-0xFB715B pushes length 2 and the pointer to the {checksum, 0xF7} pair. Buffer layout +0x0E = first message byte is fixed by sub_FB7FEB 0xFB7FEB, which sets the +0x02/+0x06/+0x0A pointers all to buf+0x0E, and by sub_FB7165, which transmits from buf+0x0E.

findings.topic: Block size: 0xFC message bytes, so 120 or 125 source bytes per frame
findings.detail: The packer stops as soon as the message byte count reaches 0xFC (252). A first frame carries the 12-byte header, so 120 source bytes (240 nibble bytes) and the whole frame is 255 bytes on the wire. A continuation frame carries the 3-byte header F0 50 7E, so 125 source bytes (250 nibble bytes) and the frame is exactly 256 bytes.

findings.topic: Continuation frames re-open with F0 50 7E
findings.detail: Only the first frame of a transfer carries the full F0 50 2D 04 dd 11 <addr> <size> header. Every later frame of the same transfer begins F0 50 7E and then goes straight into nibble data. The firmware decides this from the PREVIOUS frame's continuation flag, which it also records in byte +0x0F of that frame's descriptor.

findings.topic: Continuation flag semantics, and the two frame loops
findings.detail: sub_FB6F6B (0xFB6F6B) is the ordinary frame loop: it emits frames until the transfer's remaining-byte counter (0x60FD00) hits 0, and its flag byte is 1 while bytes remain, 0 on the very last frame. sub_FB6FB2 (0xFB6FB2) is the streamed variant used for the categories whose source is fetched from the other CPU in blocks; it always emits flag = 1, because another block always follows. Categories whose source is streamed therefore end through sub_FB6F6B, so the last frame of the whole transfer still carries flag = 0.

findings.evidence: sub_FB70AE loads 1 into the stack temp and replaces it with 0 when `(0x60FD00)` is zero; sub_FB70E6 always loads 1 and never tests. Remote_E80000_Read32Blocks runs 31 loop passes of {link read, sub_FB7649, sub_FB6FB2} then one more block terminated by `call 0xF4123C` and `call sub_FB6F6B`; sub_FB26E7 does the same with 15 passes plus one.

findings.topic: Handshake: a two-message enquiry before any data, retried three times each
findings.detail: sub_FB2323 runs at the start of every dump job, before any data. Step 1: send F0 50 21 04 00 11 F7 and wait for a reply whose parsed class is 8 — i.e. an incoming F0 50 22 04 <00|01> 11 F7. It retries up to 3 times; if all three fail it clears the error field and carries on WITHOUT the ACK protocol. On success it copies the reply's bytes at offsets 4, 5, 6 (parse-record fields 6, 7, 8) into RAM 0x60FC90/91/92 — the remote device's id triple. Step 2: send F0 50 22 04 00 11 F7 and wait for class 1 — an incoming F0 50 23 7E F7 (ACK). Up to 3 attempts. On success it sets bit 7 of (0x60FD40), which is the flag that turns on per-frame acknowledgement for the rest of the dump.
findings.symbols: sub_FB2323 0xFB2323, templates 0xF4FED5 and 0xF4FEDC, sub_FB6072 0xFB6072, sub_FB62D3 0xFB62D3, (0x60FD40) bit 7
findings.evidence: 0xFB2334/0xFB233A append 7 bytes from 0xF4FED5 via sub_FB6E7F (which auto-transmits because the last byte is 0xF7); 0xFB2355 `cp A,0x08`; 0xFB235C `cp h,0x03 / jr c` bounds the retries. 0xFB23AD/0xFB23B3 append 0xF4FEDC; 0xFB23CE `cp a,0x01`; 0xFB23D2 `set 7,(0x60FD40)`. The class values come from the receive trie at prom_b 0xF5115B: F0 50 22 04 {00|01} 11 -> class 8 (terminal at 0xF4FF91), F0 50 23 7E -> class 1 (root entry 0xF51167).

findings.topic: Per-frame acknowledgement, retransmission and the two timeouts
findings.detail: After every data frame is handed to the MIDI output, sub_FB6026 runs. If bit 7 of (0x60FD40) is set (the handshake succeeded) it waits for a reply and requires class 1, i.e. F0 50 23 7E F7. Class 6 sets the status byte to 0x1F and gives up. Anything else causes the SAME frame to be retransmitted from the other buffer (0x60FC8C) through sub_FB7165, up to 3 attempts; after 3 the status byte becomes 0x18 and the session aborts. If bit 7 is clear (no handshake partner), no ACK is expected at all: it just spins until the MIDI-out ring is empty and then waits 0x19 = 25 timer-1 ticks (~51 ms at the 488.28 Hz of notes/FINDINGS-system-clock.md) before the next frame. The reply wait itself times out after 0x09C4 = 2500 ticks (~5.1 s), or 0x03E8 = 1000 ticks (~2.05 s) when bit 2 of (0x60FD40) is set, which sub_FB2323 sets around each handshake send; on expiry the status byte becomes 5.

findings.evidence: 0xFB602D `bit 7,(0x60FD40)`; 0xFB603D `cp h,0x01 / jr z` done; 0xFB6041 `cp h,0x06` -> `ld (XBC+0x04),0x1f`; 0xFB6053 `calr` to 0xFB7165 with (0x60FC8C) pushed; 0xFB6059 `cp l,0x03 / jr c`; 0xFB6063 `ld (XBC+0x04),0x18`. 0xFB6069 is the no-handshake arm: Ring601432_SpinUntilEmpty then sub_FB77C7, whose loop is `cp BC,0x0019 / jr lt` on the free-running tick (0x0080). sub_FB7785 `ldw hl,0x09C4` / `ldw hl,0x03E8` under `bit 2,(0x60FD40)`, then status field 4 = 5 on expiry.

findings.topic: End-of-category, end-of-dump and abort messages
findings.detail: After each category finishes, sub_FB277E bumps the step id and sends F0 50 27 7E F7, then waits for the ACK. After the whole job, sub_FB27AD sends F0 50 28 7E F7 and waits. If the status byte comes back 0x18 (three failed retries), it then sends F0 50 29 7E F7 — the abort/gave-up notification.

findings.topic: The same protocol in reverse — what the WSA1R answers when it is the receiver
findings.detail: When the machine is on the receiving end, sub_FB28BE generates the acknowledgement, but only while bit 7 of (0x60FD40) is set. Status byte 0 -> F0 50 23 7E F7 (ACK). Status byte 0x16 -> F0 50 2A 7E F7. Any other status -> F0 50 24 7E F7 (NAK). An incoming F0 50 21 04 dd 11 F7 (class 7) is answered at 0xFB28FF by sending F0 50 22 04 00 11 F7, which confirms that the 0x22 message is the reply to the 0x21 enquiry.

findings.evidence: 0xFB28CF `ld H,(XBC+0x04)`; 0xFB28D9 `lda xwa,(0xF4FEB4)`; 0xFB28E4 `cp H,0x16` -> 0xFB28E9 `lda xbc,(0xF4FECD)`; else 0xFB28F1 `lda xbc,(0xF4FEB9)`. Table 0xF4F916 entry 7 = 0x00FB28FF and entry 8 = 0x00FB291D; 0xFB290D-0xFB2916 appends 7 bytes of 0xF4FEDC.

findings.topic: The complete command byte vocabulary the firmware will parse
findings.detail: The receive trie at prom_b 0xF5115B accepts exactly 14 command bytes in the third position after F0 50: 0x21, 0x22, 0x23, 0x24, 0x25, 0x27, 0x28, 0x29, 0x2A, 0x2B, 0x2C, 0x2D, 0x7E, 0x7F. Terminal classes are: 23 7E -> 1; 24 7E -> 2; 27 7E -> 3; 28 7E and 2A 7E -> 4; 29 7E -> 5; 21 04 dd 11 -> 7; 22 04 dd 11 -> 8; 25 -> 9; 7E -> 0x0A; the eight 2D data headers -> 0x0B, 0x0C, 0x0E, 0x12, 0x13, 0x14, 0x15, 0x16; 2C 04 dd 11 <3-byte parameter id> -> 0x18 (3618 accepted parameter ids); 2B 04 dd 11 <3-byte parameter id> -> 0x1A (3612 ids); 7F 09 01 -> 0x20 and 7F 09 02 -> 0x21. Note that the anomalous template F0 50 2D 04 00 11 20 00 00 00 00 10 at prom_b 0xF4FF10 is NOT in the grammar and belongs to the unreferenced routine at 0xFB248A.
findings.symbols: trie root prom_b 0xF5115B, sub_FB63D1 0xFB63D1, sub_FB61B1 0xFB61B1, wsa1/notes/sysex-probes/sysex_grammar_dump.py
findings.evidence: 0xFB63FC `add XBC,0x00F5115B`, bounded to 15 records by `ld l,0x0f` at 0xFB63F2 and `dec 1,L` at 0xFB649A, stride 6 from `inc 6,DE`. Record = [0] match byte, [1] class (0 = descend), [2..5] LE32 next node; 0xFF ends a node, 0xFE is a wildcard. Walked exhaustively from the ROM image.

findings.topic: The receiver only accepts messages that begin F0 50
findings.detail: The byte-level SysEx collector rejects anything whose first byte is not 0xF0 (status code 1) or whose second byte is not 0x50 (status code 2). A status byte other than 0xF7 arriving mid-message gives code 3, and a message of 0xFF bytes or more gives code 6. So this machine ignores every other maker's SysEx in the bulk-dump path. Which company holds manufacturer id 0x50 is NOT established anywhere in this tree — do not write a company name into the manual on the strength of the byte alone.
findings.symbols: sub_FB6098 0xFB6098, sub_FB6165 0xFB6165, MIDI_RX_SysExStart 0xFA584D
findings.evidence: 0xFB60E0 `cp H,0xF0`, 0xFB60EE `cp H,0x50`, 0xFB612C `cp H,0xF7`, 0xFB610A `cp WA,0x00FF`. The interrupt-side parser MIDI_RX_SysExStart independently accepts only identifier bytes 0x50 and 0x7E (notes/FINDINGS-midi-port.md, which also records the searched negative about the company name).

findings.topic: How a frame reaches the wire, and which port
findings.detail: sub_FB7165 (0xFB7165) writes the finished frame into MIDI-out ring 0x601432 in 0x20-byte chunks through prom_b thunk 0xF41DF8 (T_Ring601432_PutBlock), calling 0xF40724 (T_MIDI_PostSendWork) after each chunk, with `ei 6` / `ei 0` bracketing each chunk. It also writes 0x00 to the one-byte mailbox (0x9B) first. Ring 0x601432 is the queue MIDI_TX_Ready drains into SC0BUF, i.e. MIDI OUT. A sibling, sub_FB71BB (0xFB71BB), sends the same frame to BOTH 0x601432 and the second ring 0x60153C (T_Ring60153C_PutBlock 0xF41E1C, woken through T_MIDI_PostSendWork_PortB 0xF40730); the bulk-dump frame loops use sub_FB7165 only.
findings.symbols: sub_FB7165 0xFB7165, sub_FB71BB 0xFB71BB, T_Ring601432_PutBlock 0xF41DF8, T_MIDI_PostSendWork 0xF40724, Ring601432_Get 0xF847F7, MIDI_TX_Ready 0xFA542F
findings.evidence: 0xFB7189 and 0xFB71AA `call 0xF41DF8` with the pushed length 0x20 and then HL; prom_b line 82805 `T_Ring601432_PutBlock: jp 0xF8481C`. notes/FINDINGS-midi-port.md establishes that MIDI_TX_Ready pulls from the output queue through 0xF41DF0 = T_Ring601432_Get.

findings.topic: Per-category transfer breakdown as it appears on the wire
findings.detail: SYSTEM,PART & MIDI = two transfers: address 0x100000 size 32 bytes (RAM 0x7600-0x761F) and address 0x100020 size 2400 bytes (RAM 0x7620-0x7F7F); 2432 bytes total. SOUND = one transfer: address 0x080000 size 262144 bytes, streamed from the other CPU's 0xE80000-0xEBFFFF in 32 blocks of 8 KiB through the staging buffer at 0x60A000. COMBINATION = two transfers: address 0x140000 size 768 bytes (remote 0xEC0000) and address 0x140300 size 90112 bytes (remote 0xEC0300 upward in 16 blocks of 0x1600); 0x16300 total. SEQUENCER = three transfers: address 0x180000 size 3072 (RAM 0x603400), address 0x180C00 size 30720 (RAM 0x610000), address 0x188400 with a run-time size (RAM from 0x617800; the static form is 0x50C00, but with bit 6 of (0x60FD40) set — which the UI path always sets — the size becomes the word at 0x603452 times 16).
findings.symbols: sub_FB23EF/sub_FB23F9/sub_FB243E, Remote_E80000_Read32Blocks 0xFB24EC, sub_FB2675/sub_FB267F/sub_FB26E7, sub_FB2587/sub_FB25A2/sub_FB25E7/sub_FB262C, descriptor writers sub_FB75BA/FB75E4/FB7649/FB766F/FB7692/FB76B5/FB76F2/FB7722, sub_FB7748 0xFB7748

findings.topic: The buffers and the parse record, for anyone re-deriving this
findings.detail: Two 280-byte transmit buffers at 0x60FA50 and 0x60FB68 (current pointer in 0x60FC88, spare in 0x60FC8C) and two receive buffers at 0x60F820/0x60F938 (0x60FC80/0x60FC84). Buffer layout: +0 word = message byte count, +2 long = parse cursor, +6 long, +0x0A long = write cursor, +0x0E onward = the message bytes, with a 0xFF sentinel written at the cursor after every append. Four 16-byte descriptors at 0x60FCB8/0x60FCC8 (transmit, pointers in 0x60FCE0/0x60FCE4) and 0x60FC98/0x60FCA8 (receive, 0x60FCD8/0x60FCDC); field 0 = parsed message class, field 3 = step id, field 4 = status/error, fields 5..0x0E = the matched header bytes, field 0x0F = the last continuation flag. The transfer descriptor is the triple at 0x60FCF8 (current source pointer), 0x60FCFC (end pointer), 0x60FD00 (remaining bytes).
findings.symbols: sub_FB7F42 0xFB7F42 (the allocator), sub_FB7FEB 0xFB7FEB (buffer init, descriptor template prom_b 0xF511E9), sub_FB6219 0xFB6219 (field setter), sub_FB62D3 0xFB62D3 (field getter), sub_FB8081 0xFB8081 / sub_FB8028 0xFB8028 (the buffer swaps)
findings.evidence: sub_FB7F42 is a run of `lda` / `ld (0x60FCxx),xbc` pairs naming every address above; sub_FB7FEB sets +0x02, +0x06 and +0x0A all to XIX+0x0E and writes 0xFF there, then `ldirw` 8 words from 0xF511E9 into the descriptor. sub_FB6219/sub_FB62D3 are 16-way jump tables over offsets +0..+0x0F (JumpTable_FB6240, JumpTable_FB62F6), each with the last-entry test already recorded in the .s headers.

findings.topic: The 2B / 2C messages are single-parameter traffic, not bulk dump
findings.detail: F0 50 2C 04 dd 11 <3-byte parameter id> <value...> F7 and F0 50 2B 04 dd 11 <3-byte parameter id> ... F7 share the same F0 50 <cmd> 04 dd 11 envelope but are parameter messages, dispatched to 0xFB34CA and 0xFB42AB rather than to the bulk-dump handlers. The bare 6-byte template at prom_b 0xF4FEF2 = F0 50 2C 04 00 11 is the header those transmit sites prepend. Which of the two is the SET and which the REQUEST is not established here.
findings.symbols: template prom_b 0xF4FEF2, transmit sites 0xFB47E9, 0xFB48E7, 0xFB4A59, 0xFB4DAF, 0xFB4E65, 0xFB4F26, 0xFB4FDC, 0xFB53BF, 0xFB5473; dispatch table prom_b 0xF4F800 entries 0x18 and 0x1A
findings.evidence: The trie assigns class 0x18 to 3618 distinct 2C forms and 0x1A to 3612 distinct 2B forms, all of shape 04 <00|01> 11 followed by a three-byte id. Table 0xF4F800[0x18] = 0x00FB34CA, [0x1A] = 0x00FB42AB.

findings.topic: Remote-triggered dumps use the same engine
findings.detail: Five code arms at 0xFB5122, 0xFB512C, 0xFB5136, 0xFB5140 and 0xFB514A set (0x60F802) to 4, 3, 1, 2 and 5 and then call sub_FB516A, which runs the job immediately only when the current screen (0x207A) is 0x79 — the SYSEX BULK DUMP screen — or when (0x2076)==1 and (0x207A)==1; otherwise it sets the status byte to 0x11. These five arms are entries 0x1B..0x1F of both 34-entry message dispatch tables at prom_b 0xF4F800 and 0xF4F888.
findings.symbols: 0xFB5122-0xFB514A, sub_FB516A 0xFB516A, sub_FB5154 0xFB5154, dispatch tables prom_b 0xF4F800 / 0xF4F888
findings.evidence: 0xFB516A `cp (0x207A),0x79 / jr z` then `cp (0x2076),0x01` and `cp (0x207A),0x01`; 0xFB5184 pushes 0x11 into field 4. Table entries read from the ROM image at 0xF4F86C..0xF4F87C and 0xF4F8F4..0xF4F904. ⚠ No form in the trie at 0xF5115B produces classes 0x1B..0x1F, so which incoming message reaches these arms is NOT established.

openQuestions: Which incoming SysEx message actually selects a category for a remote-triggered dump. The five arms at 0xFB5122-0xFB514A are dispatch-table entries 0x1B..0x1F, but the receive trie at prom_b 0xF5115B produces no form with those classes. Either a second grammar root exists or those classes are raised internally; neither was found. UNVERIFIED — do not publish a "dump request" message format.
The class-6 arm of sub_FB6026 (0xFB6041 `cp h,0x06` -> status 0x1F). No byte sequence in the trie yields class 6, so the wire form that triggers it is UNVERIFIED.

Press/release semantics. PanelButton_Route (0xF861AC) passes the button index in W bits 0-4 and a flag in bit 7; the existing header reads bit 7 clear as "released", but that word is not cited to anything. On screen 0x79 the four row-select handlers act with bit 7 SET while the dump-start arm of 0xF99A8F acts with bit 7 CLEAR, and on the GENERAL MIDI screen (0xF99DDD, 0xF99DF4, 0xF99E2C) every handler acts with bit 7 CLEAR. Which physical panel key is index 9 — and whether the on-screen " SEND" label belongs to it or to index 15 (0xF99B6E, which only requests screen 0x12) — is UNVERIFIED.

What the constant bytes 0x04 and 0x11 mean. They are in every 21/22/2B/2C/2D message and the trie matches them literally. A product-family byte and a model id is the obvious reading but nothing in the ROM says so. Likewise nothing says whether a user can ever make the machine transmit device number 0x01 rather than 0x00; every transmit template holds 0x00 and only the receiver accepts either.

The address space. 0x080000 (SOUND), 0x100000 (SYSTEM,PART & MIDI), 0x140000 (COMBINATION), 0x180000/0x188400 (SEQUENCER) are logical addresses that do not equal the internal source addresses (RAM 0x7600, remote flash 0xE80000/0xEC0000). Whether they map onto anything a user or a service manual would recognise is UNVERIFIED.

(0xC4). Its value 1 enables the SEQUENCER dump and 2 hides the SEQUENCER row entirely; a model or option variant is the obvious reading, but it is not established. This matters for the manual: on a machine where (0xC4) != 1 the SEQUENCER category is silently refused.

The second output ring 0x60153C, woken through T_MIDI_PostSendWork_PortB (0xF40730 -> 0xFA5C12). It looks like a second MIDI OUT, and sub_FB71BB sends to both rings, but no bulk-dump frame goes through it and the port's identity is UNVERIFIED.

The one-byte mailbox (0x9B), set to 0x00 by both sub_FB7165 and sub_FB71BB and to 0xF3 at 0xFE1507. notes/FINDINGS-midi-port.md records it as selecting an arm of MIDI_PostSendWork but does not decode it.

The orphan at 0xFB248A and its template prom_b 0xF4FF10 (F0 50 2D 04 00 11 20 00 00 00 00 10). Nothing names 0xFB248A, and its template says 16 bytes while the routine passes count 0x0000 to the link read. It should NOT go into the manual as a real message; the probe asserts the anomaly so it will fire if either half changes.

Frame timing on the wire. A 256-byte frame exactly fills the 0x100-byte MIDI-out ring and Ring_Put_0100 drops rather than blocks, so whether a real transfer ever loses a byte depends on interrupt latency, which cannot be settled from the disassembly. Felipe's hardware is unreachable (notes: kn5000-hardware-inaccessible), so this is a hardware question to park.
